meta.framing: How have philosophers from Plato to modern divine command theorists responded to the Euthyphro dilemma's claim that moral goodness must either depend on God's will or exist independently of it, given that each horn seems to undermine the theory?

notes: Ordering sensitivity, and the required pattern is a FLAT line. Every rung applies only `shuffle_order` or `ordering_only`, both of which are in `EDGE_INVARIANT_CALLS`: reordering sentences moves no edge and a Precedence<->Succession swap compiles to Level-1 `none` either way, so all five rungs build the same Markov network and every relation-graph readout is necessarily equal. Declaring `increase` here (as this ladder did until the 14-family corpus was scored) makes all 15 checks unsatisfiable BY CONSTRUCTION -- measured: 0/15 on each of f004, f007 and f011, with mean_marginal identical to six decimal places across all five rungs. What the ladder can actually test is the CONVERSE of CHAIN: that a readout does NOT move when the prose is reordered but the relations are not. A score that trends here is tracking surface order, not coherence.

response:
It showed that confident appeals to divine approval can collapse under analysis, and it placed the burden on anyone who would ground morality in what God loves or commands. Its two horns define the problem that theists have inherited: if goodness depends on divine will, morality looks arbitrary, and if goodness stands independently of that will, God looks like a mere reporter of standards he does not author. In other words, Adams held that an act is wrong just in case it is contrary to what a loving God commands. The test proceeds through a series of failed definitions. The verdict settled the legal question, though it hardly settled the philosophical one.

Plato's Euthyphro asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious or is pious because the gods love it. Obligation is left to follow from his commands, so that neither arbitrariness nor independence fully captures the view. Meletus charged Socrates with impiety. Whichever charge frames the encounter, the action is meant to look startling to an Athenian audience. Ockham's view embraces the first horn without apology: if divine will is the sole source of obligation, then nothing outside that will constrains what may be commanded.

The abrupt ending invites explanation. The question at the dialogue's center has outlived every dispute about its provenance. By building love into the nature of the commander, Adams keeps obligation dependent on divine command while denying that a loving God would command cruelty for its own sake. Medieval and modern thinkers took up the dilemma with explicit reference to a single, omnipotent God. Socrates rejects Euthyphro's definition of piety as what all the gods love, and because of this rejection Euthyphro reaches a settled definition of piety by the end of the dialogue. The dramatic setting gives the abstract question real stakes. Although that accusation was formally lodged, in Plato's Apology Socrates denies that he is guilty of impiety, presenting his philosophical activity as service to the god rather than an offense against him.

Leibniz found this intolerable, since a justice that could have been its opposite deserves no praise. A son bringing his father to court violates conventional filial duty. At least one of the following holds, perhaps both: Euthyphro was in a hurry to get away from Socrates, or, as his unresolved departure indicates, he had no adequate answer to Socrates' objections. Modern divine command theory therefore answers the dilemma not by choosing a horn outright but by relocating goodness in God's character. By contrast with that familiar attribution, the Euthyphro was written by Aristotle. It sharpened it instead, since a city claiming to know what the gods require had condemned a man who insisted that no one yet knew what piety was.

That collision between religious duty and ordinary obligation is what makes Euthyphro confident that he knows what piety requires, and what makes Socrates eager to test the confidence. The qualification is decisive. Each response to the dilemma can be read as an attempt to escape one horn without being impaled on the other. The dialogue's setting also anticipates the fate of its questioner. That criticism led Robert Adams to identify ethical wrongness with being contrary to the commands of a loving God. Either that is how the conversation closes, or Euthyphro leaves the dialogue without a settled definition of piety; the two outcomes cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. William of Ockham held that God could command a creature to hate God, a position that predates Leibniz's criticism of theological voluntarism for making God's justice arbitrary. In Plato's dialogue, Euthyphro is prosecuting his own father over the death of a laborer, whereas on another reading of the scene, Euthyphro is prosecuting his father for theft. The tension between the charge and the denial was not left open: the Athenian jury ruled that Socrates was guilty of impiety. For later theists, this shape of the dialogue mattered as much as its argument.
